Cell.Data: In the Secret Test Kitchen, you have total creative freedom to combine your ingredients in new and interesting ways to create recipes never seen before.

Bring a sample of the ingredients you collect to your Secret Test Kitchen, where they will be kept in stock for your experiments. Small gray bottles hold places for ingredients you have yet to collect.

To create a recipe, select a product category from the bulletin board. You can now customize your recipe's complexity by adding or removing ingredient bowls using the (+/-) buttons! Chocolates support 2 to 6 ingredients, while Coffees utilize 3 to 5. Click drawers to place ingredients, and click a full bowl to clear it.

To create a recipe, select a product category from the bulletin board. You can now customize your recipe's complexity by adding or removing ingredient bowls using the (+/-) buttons! Chocolate categories support 2 to 6 ingredients. Drinks use 3 to 4, while Beverage Blends use 3 to 5. Click drawers to place ingredients, and click a full bowl to clear it.

Click "%invent_taste%" to get specific, detailed flavor critiques from Teddy. Pay close attention to his feedback on your pairings! Make adjustments and click "%design_recipe%" when you're ready to move on to the next step.

You do not currently have any spaces available in the recipe book for your own recipes.

With your continued success, the Board of Directors will provide more spaces so you can create (and sell) your own inventions.
It looks like you have some ingredients we haven't seen before. We'll grab one sack of each so it will be available for use in our test kitchens.
Excellent, you've brought fresh discoveries! I'll take a sample of each new item for the archives so we can start experimenting immediately.
Oh! I don't recognize some of these ingredients. Thank you, <player>. Once we've catalogued them, they'll stay stocked in the test kitchen for anything you dream up.
Well, well - new supplies. Perfect. We'll set aside one sack of each for the kitchen pantry. New ingredients mean new trouble to get into.
You keep giving me excuses to rearrange these cupboards, <player>! As always, I shall take a sack of each unfamiliar ingredient and add them to the test kitchen stores.
Welcome back to Iceland, <player>. And you brought more ingredients with you! That's just what I wanted to see. Just let me take care of that for a second, and I'll get back to you...

You do not currently have any spaces available in the recipe book for your own recipes.

With your continued success, the Board of Directors will provide more spaces so you can create, and of course sell, your own inventions. Would you like to come inside anyway?

I'm afraid our recipe book is currently full, . Until you impress the Board enough to earn another slot, we can't officially register any new inventions.

Of course, we can still play around and work out some new taste combos while you're here. Want to come inside?

Every one of your current recipe spaces is spoken for. Until the Board grants you another, anything we invent today will have to remain unofficial. Annoying, I know.

We can certainly taste a few ideas anyway, though. Shall we?

So here's the bad news: every recipe slot the Board has given you is occupied. But the good news: nobody said we had to stop experimenting. You won't be able to save a new invention yet, but you're welcome to come inside and test ideas.

Way to go! You have completed the entire recipe book!

While you won't be able to add any more recipes, you are certainly welcome to poke around and experiment as much as you wish.

Would you like to step inside now?

Well, would you look at that? Every custom recipe space is filled. You've built quite a collection, !

Nothing says we can't keep mixing things together for the fun of it, though. Shall we head inside?

Oh! So this is -->1<--. All right, <player>, let's see what the community has been cooking up.
Someone else has done the inventing for once! -->1<-- is loaded.
-->1<--, hmm? I do enjoy borrowing other people's homework when it's this delicious.
Well, this should be interesting. I've reconstructed -->1<-- from the Community Cookbook. All ingredients are ready.
Wait a moment... -->1<-- is ours! You've brought our own work back through the Community Cookbook.
Oh! -->1<--. I know this one - we sent it out into the community ourselves. That's delightfully circular.
Ah... how lovely is it to see our very own -->1<-- back in our kitchen, <player>?
So -->6<-- is responsible for -->1<--? All right. Let's see what kind of trouble they've sent to Iceland.
-->6<--... huh. I recognize that name from the Cookbook. This is their -->1<--, then.
This is familiar territory! I've reconstructed -->1<-- exactly as it was shared.
A bar called -->1<--, hmm? No foams, no fancy cups, nowhere for a bad pairing to hide. Let's taste it.
Chocolate bars look simple until you try to make a memorable one. I'm curious what they've done this guy right here.
Oh, good! I was beginning to worry the Community Cookbook had forgotten what company we work for.
Coffee! Excellent. -->1<-- is loaded and, purely in the interest of science, I am prepared to taste as many caffeinated samples as necessary.
Now this is speaking my language. -->1<-- is a coffee creation, and roasted beans are really honest about what you put beside them.
A community coffee recipe, hmm? Put -->1<-- in front of me and suddenly this feels like a very productive morning.
Coffee is a wonderful test medium: bitter, aromatic, unforgiving. -->1<-- is ready.
A drink! Good. -->1<-- is on the bench. Coffee, chocolate, fruit, tea, milk... I don't care which road it took here as long as it tastes good.
Now we're talking. -->1<-- is a drink, so the important question is whether I'd ask for a second glass.
A community drink, hmm? All right. Cup, straw, spoon, whatever this thing needs... let's taste it.
Drinks are wonderfully unforgiving. One bad ingredient has nowhere to hide. -->1<-- is ready.
A beverage blend. Excellent. -->1<-- is ready. Grounds, leaves, powder... let's see whether the mix knows what it wants to become.
A packaged blend, huh? Good. Coffee, chai, cocoa, tea... the bag can say whatever it likes; the cup still has to taste good.
Ah, -->1<-- is a blend. We're judging the mixture before it ever reaches the customer's cupboard. Let's be picky.
Beverage blends are all about proportion. Too much of one thing and every cup from the packet inherits the mistake.
An infusion! Delicate business. One good ingredient and it's elegant, but one bad one and it tastes like a cupboard.
So -->1<-- is an infusion? We'll have to see whether the recipe whispers nicely or starts shouting.
Tea leaves, herbs, chocolate... an infusion can go in so many directions. -->1<-- has my attention.
I tell you, <player>... Truffles always take me back to the glory days of Baumeister Confections. I just love those small delights.
Truffles tend to come with rich fillings and concentrated flavors. Let's see what -->1<-- is made of and hope it comes out just right!
A community truffle recipe? Good. These classics demand a delicate hand, don't they?
A coffee blend. Excellent. -->1<-- is ready, and I intend to be extremely particular about the balance.
Blends are where people discover that 'more coffee' is not the same as 'better coffee.' Let's see what -->1<-- does.
Ah, -->1<-- is a blend. Aroma first, structure second, then everything else. Let's taste before we change a thing.
Coffee blends are a lovely little exercise in controlled obsession. Whoever made -->1<-- has my attention.
-->1<-- could be brilliant or completely unhinged. Either outcome is interesting.
The Exotic category is basically a signed permission slip for risky ideas, which occasionally become excellent ideas. -->1<-- is ready.
Well, -->1<-- certainly isn't playing it safe. Good.
An Exotic creation from the community! All right, <player>, no assumptions. We taste first and ask difficult questions afterward.
Well, well. -->1<-- is averaging -->3<-- out of five from -->4<-- ratings. The community seems rather convinced! Naturally, I intend to verify their findings myself.
-->1<-- has a -->3<-- rating? That's close to a consensus, <player>. We should taste it!
Apparently -->1<-- is one of the popular children: -->3<-- out of five across -->4<-- ratings. Let's see what all the fuss is about...
A -->2<-- with a -->3<-- average from -->4<-- ratings? Those are respectable numbers.
Oof. -->1<-- is averaging -->3<-- out of five from -->4<-- ratings. The community has been rather unkind, huh?
Only -->3<-- out of five for -->1<--? So either we've found a disaster or a misunderstood masterpiece.
-->1<-- has not exactly charmed the public: -->3<-- out of five across -->4<-- ratings. I want to know why.
A -->2<-- sitting at -->3<-- out of five. Hmm. Poor thing. Let's give -->1<-- a fair hearing before we start rearranging its ingredients.
-->1<-- has been loaded -->5<-- times already? Apparently we're not the first people to get curious. Well, we have to see whether the crowd was onto something.
This recipe gets around! -->1<-- has been pulled into other Test Kitchens -->5<-- times. I suppose we'd better conduct our own independent review.
-->5<-- loads for -->1<--. That's enough repetition to make me suspicious of a trend. Excellent.
Oh, and the creator tagged -->1<-- as Experimental. That's either admirable honesty or a warning label. I like both.
Experimental, is it? Good. If I wanted predictable, I wouldn't be standing in a laboratory with chocolate stains on my coat.
-->1<-- comes with an Experimental tag. Wonderful. At least nobody can claim we weren't warned.
Boozy, according to the tag. Fine. We shall proceed with the utmost scientific professionalism and absolutely no second samples.
Ah. The creator marked -->1<-- as Boozy. I suddenly understand why this recipe has such confidence.
Boozy? In the Test Kitchen? For research purposes, obviously. Very serious research.
Savoury? That's bold. Chocolate and coffee don't always enjoy sharing the room with dinner, but I'm willing to hear -->1<-- out.
The Savoury tag is staring at me like a dare. All right, -->1<--, you have my attention.
A savoury creation. Interesting. This is exactly how afternoons in this laboratory get complicated.
Tropical! In Iceland! Excellent. -->1<-- may be the closest thing we're getting to sunshine in this room today.
The creator calls -->1<-- Tropical. Fruit, perfume, acidity... what would this one bring?
Tropical, hmm? Good. If the weather outside refuses to cooperate, we'll manufacture our own climate on the tasting bench.
Select the ingredients to use from the drawers. Click %invent_taste% and we'll give you some feedback on what you've got.
You should give your new recipe a name and a description before adding it permanently to your recipe book.
There is already a recipe with that name. Why not choose another name so you don't confuse your customers?

Select the ingredients to use from the drawers. Click %invent_taste% and we'll give you some feedback on what you've got.
Pick your ingredients from the drawers and fill the bowls on the bench. When you're ready, click %invent_taste% and I'll tell you exactly what I think.
The pantry's yours, <player>. Build your combination in the bowls and press %invent_taste% when you're ready to let me try it.
Choose the ingredients you want to test, then use %invent_taste% when you're satisfied with your combinations. I'll give you my verdict.
You should give your new recipe a name and a description before adding it permanently to your recipe book.
Hold on, you forgot the marketing! Fill in the name and description fields before we file this.
Wait, wait... what are we calling it? And what are we telling people it is? Please give the recipe a name and description before we put it in the book.
There is already a recipe with that name. Why not choose another name so you don't confuse your customers?
We already have a "%1%" in the recipe book. You need a fresh name for a fresh creation.
Deiter would have my head if we had two products with the same name, and we've already got one of those %1%. Try something original.
Are you sure you want to add this recipe to our recipe book? Adding a recipe will permanently use up one of your available spaces.
This looks excellent. Are you ready to commit this to the recipe book? It will consume one of your custom slots permanently.
I think we've got ourselves a finished recipe. If you're certain, I'll write it into the book - but remember, once that space is used, we're not getting it back.
All right, <player>, this is the point of no return. Are we ready to publish this delicacy to the world and fill up a spot in your recipe book?
You have to fill all of the available ingredient slots for us to prepare your recipe for tasting.
You can't leave bowls out on the bench here for nothing, <player>. Choose some more ingredients, or add and remove bowls to the right of the screen.
Don't be lazy, <player>! You'll need to fill all bowls with ingredients so I can taste and give you the feedback you need.
I can't taste air, <player>. Fill all the slots or use the (-) button to reduce the recipe size.
I'm willing to taste almost anything you make, but an empty bowl isn't much of a recipe. Fill every slot first.
We're missing at least one ingredient. Please put something in every bowl or use the (-) button to shorten the recipe.
This is exactly the same as the last one. I assure you, it hasn't improved with age. Try changing an ingredient.
Again? Really? My feedback hasn't changed. C'mon, experiment a little!
Okay, this isn't funny anymore. It's still a bad recipe. Are you even listening to me?
Please, <player>. I need something nice to taste. Give me something different!
My palate has perfect recall, <player>. The answer is still the same as it was ten seconds ago, don't you know?
Unless you swap something out, stop asking me to taste the exact same thing.
Mm-hm. Still the same. Swap something out and then call me over.
Are we waiting for the ingredients to change themselves, <player>, or...?
This looks just like your recipe for %1%.
Silly! You already have this registered as %1% in your recipe book.
If I were you, <player>, I wouldn't waste a valuable blank page in the recipe book just to recreate %1%. Be original!
You may have forgot about it, but you already have this recipe named %1% that uses these ingredients together.
My taste buds are having déjà vu. You've already got this exact combination written down as %1%.
Tasty? Yes. Original? No. You already know this one as %1%.
We've been there, done that, and printed the label. That's just your %1% recipe again. Try something new.
You're repeating yourself, <player>. This is exactly the same as your %1%.
Mm... wait. I know this. This is %1%, isn't it?
I once saw a recipe for a product like this somewhere else. You might want to ask around and see if someone already knows it.
I suspect this recipe already exists out in the world. Ask around before you try to claim it as your own, <player>.
You may want to hold up on using these ingredients together, because there may be a recipe out there that's probably just what you're looking for...
Don't get me wrong, this tastes great. But I have a hunch this recipe is already out there. You might want to ask around and do some favors. You know, see if you can acquire it from a local first.
It's technically competent, sure. But I'm pretty sure I tasted this exact thing last year. Someone may have a recipe for us out there.
I've seen this recipe out in the wild before. We need something that screams 'Baumeister,' not 'Generic Store Brand'.
This combination works for me! Click %invent_design% to design, name and describe your creation!
Mm! Yeah, that works. I wouldn't change a thing. If you want it in the book, click %invent_design%.
Oh, that's good! That's actually very good. Go on - %invent_design%.
I think you've got it, <player>. Click %invent_design% and let's turn this into a proper recipe.
This combination works for me! But you'll need an additional space in our recipe book to actually create one of these.
Oh, that's good. Shame we've got nowhere to write it down yet. Put a lid on this idea and we can come back to it another time.
That's a keeper... except we can't keep it. Not until the Board gives you another slot.
I'd approve this one. We just need somewhere to put it first - come back when you've got another recipe space.
Have a smell of those Balinese beans, <player>. Volcanic soil, citrus growing nearby - no wonder there's so much going on in them. Treat them gently and they'll tell you plenty.
So this is the famous Honduran bean Sean discovered? It smells... ancient. Smoky. Be careful not to overpower it with too much sugar.
Colombian nacional cacao beans are known for delicate floral notes and very low bitterness. Don't bury it under heavy spices.
Good to see you're making use of %dou_plantationkeep%'s new harvest. This robust variant is the backbone of a strong chocolate, so don't be afraid to let it shine.
Peruvian cacao! Look at the color of those beans. They are practically white inside! This is going to be a very delicate chocolate.
Madagascan beans! These are famous for their bright, red-berry acidity. It will make for a very lively, tart chocolate.
Ah, Ethiopian beans. The birthplace of coffee itself! They are wine-like, floral, and complex. Do not burn them!
Indonesian coffee's wet-hulled, which gives it that heavy, syrupy body and earthy taste.
Colombian Arabica is the definition of a balanced cup. Nutty, bright, and clean. It's hard to make a bad drink with this.
These Cuban coffee beans are dark roasted and intense. They practically demand to be whipped with sugar into a 'cafecito'.
Do you know how hard these beans are to get? It is remarkably smooth with almost zero bitterness. We must ensure the roast profile is perfect.
Coffee from the markets of Tangier, huh? It has a spicy, robust character to it. I feel awake just smelling it!
Lavender is tricky. Use too much and the chocolate tastes like soap. Use just enough, and it's perfume.
Ah, matcha. The Japanese have used this for centuries, but it's a novelty for us. I'm curious to see the color.
You've grabbed the dusting powder. That means we're making truffles! Remember, the coating is the first thing the customer tastes.
Those rose petals are very romantic. Handle them gently, we don't want to crush them.
Saffron? Do you know how much this costs per gram? Please tell me you have a plan for this and aren't just throwing money into the mixing bowl.
Sumac? That's an unusual acid profile. It's tart like lemon, but earthy. Interesting choice.
Wasabi? In a confection? You're a madman, <player>.
You won't be making too much chocolate without a base of cacao beans!
We are chocolatiers, right, <player>? Let's use some cacao.
Technically, legally, and culinarily, this isn't chocolate.
Without something to sweeten it, raw cacao has a pretty bitter taste. Try some sweetener.
Whoa! That is aggressively bitter. We need sugar or something sweet to mellow those tannins out.
Every truffle recipe must include a dusting of %powder%.
I can't hold a truffle properly without it melting instantly. It needs a coat of %powder%, or we'll have a mess on our hands.
Ah, no coating. That's why it's already melting on my fingers. Give the truffle some %powder%.
Without a little variety in your recipe, you may as well be selling raw ingredients!
Boring! My palate is falling asleep.
Complexity is the spice of life, <player>! Mix it up a little!
Is that it? One thing, over and over? Come on, give me something else to taste in there.
That recipe seems a bit heavy on the dairy. Try mixing it up a bit!
I love a creamy texture, but this is ridiculous. We need more solids to hold the structure together.
This isn't chocolate, it's a milkshake. Cut back on the liquids or it will never set properly.
Blech! That combination is far too sweet on the tongue.
My teeth hurt just looking at this. Dial back the sugar, it's drowning out the flavor of the cacao.
I think I just developed a cavity. Way, way too sweet. Balance it out.
All that flavoring masks the taste of our delicious cacao. Try toning it down a bit.
I'm tasting... everything? And nothing? It's a sensory overload. Come on, let the cacao breathe!
It tastes like I bit into a spice rack. We need a base to carry these flavors, not drown in them.
Hang on, hang on - there's too much happening. I can't pick out a single thing.
What's this? Are you making chocolate or coffee?!
This bar is vibrating on the table. If you want to make espresso, use the other factory!
Now that's chocolate with its shoulders back. Hardly any dairy, plenty of cacao, a clean bitter finish - some customers will adore it and some will run for the milk bars.
You are letting the beans speak for themselves here. No milk to hide behind!
How can you make coffee without coffee beans? Be sure to include some!
This is just a warm, flavored beverage. We are a coffee company now, too. Add some beans!
You need to actually put coffee beans in the machine, <player>...
That recipe seems a bit heavy on the dairy. Try mixing it up a bit!
This is just warm milk with a rumor of coffee. We need a stronger brew.
I ordered a latte, not a glass of hot cream.
If you put that much sugar in your coffee, you'll never taste anything but sweet!
It's basically hot syrup. Our customers want a caffeine kick, not a sugar coma.
Oh, wow. That's sweet. I lost the coffee on the first sip.
With all those competing flavors, I can barely taste the coffee in that drink. Try mixing it up.
I can't find the coffee underneath all this seasoning. You're over-engineering it!
Wait, what am I supposed to be tasting first? There's too much going on.
We can make a mocha with a little cacao, but do we really need that much?
If I wanted to drink melted chocolate, I'd go to the other factory. Less cacao, more java!
Hmm... I don't think our customers are going to appreciate that much fruit in their coffee...
We only need just a hint of fruit, not a whole fruit punch latte! Tone it down.
Have you ever had hot fruit juice mixed with espresso? No? There is a reason for that. It's awful.
Some people like nutty coffee, but that's just a metaphor. We don't use actual nuts in our coffee drinks!
I'm chewing my morning brew. That's not right. Use a liqueur if you want nut flavor, not whole nuts.
Imagine reaching the bottom of your cup and finding a soggy nut. Unpleasant, right? I assure, nobody will like that experience.
Ow - was that a nut? In the coffee? No, no, we're not doing that.
You're brewing coffee, <player>, not running an illicit distillery.
You really can't go wrong pairing coffee with chocolate. It's only natural for Baumeister Confections!
The two greatest beans in the world are natural best friends. You really can't mess this up.
This tastes like something they'd serve in a café overlooking the Mediterranean.
Give me another bite of that. The berry snaps straight through the dark cacao and leaves the chocolate tasting cleaner at the finish.
That's a berry burst of antioxidants!
I like what's happening here - a little crunch, a little smoothness. Texture contrast done right!
I, for one, am a fan of spicy chocolates!
Let me tell you a fun fact. This spicy, bitter profile is exactly how the Aztec emperors enjoyed their cacao.
Now this is a bold return to the roots of chocolate, <player>!
No dairy, high cacao, and spice... you are drinking history, <player>. This is chocolate as it was invented.
Someone open a window; this tastes like the kitchen has wandered somewhere much warmer than Iceland. Bright fruit, plenty of perfume, no apology for it.
You could put this in the front window and let the color do half the selling. It tastes every bit as cheerful as it looks.
Yum! Consumers will certainly gobble those up around the fall holidays!
This tastes like harvest season. Surely these will sell well in the fall.
Ooh, that's got some snap to it! The hibiscus gives the dark tea a sour, wine-like bite that really wakes it up.
This is just hot, cloudy milk, <player>. The tea is barely even a rumor in there!
Ugh, my teeth are buzzing. You sweetened this until the tea completely surrendered.
I mean, it's delicious, but it's just hot chocolate now. The cacao completely bullied the tea leaves into hiding.
Blech! This has a hint of battery acid.
Oh, that's a proper thick shake. Banana and peanut together... I'd need a spoon if you made it any thicker.
That's lunch disguised as dessert. Nutty, creamy, cold, and ridiculously filling.
Now you're showing off. Salted caramel in a milkshake is the sort of thing that makes people scrape the bottom of the glass.
Mm! There's the salt right at the end. Good. Otherwise this much caramel would wear me out halfway through the glass.
Cherry-vanilla shake. That tastes like something a soda fountain ought to have its name on.
Oh, I like this one. Cold vanilla, bright cherry, and a glass I absolutely intend to finish.
Chocolate shake with raspberry? Yes. That's almost a sundae that learned how to fit through a straw.
That little raspberry tang keeps the chocolate shake from turning into one long mouthful of sweetness. I'd order this.
Coffee milkshake. Breakfast has officially stopped pretending to be responsible, and I am completely fine with that.
Oh, that's good. Cold, creamy, unmistakably coffee... somebody is going to drink this far too quickly.
Pineapple and coconut in a milkshake? All right, give me the ridiculous straw and let me enjoy myself.
This has gone straight from dairy counter to holiday drink. Creamy, tropical, and extremely cheerful.
No ice cream this time? Good call. Strawberry and banana make a thick fruit drink without turning the whole thing into dessert.
Mango and coconut milkiness... that's silky. I could see this disappearing very quickly on a hot afternoon.
Blueberry, milk and honey. Simple, thick, and pleasantly breakfast-like. Not every drink needs fireworks.
Ah, there it is. Proper hot chocolate: cacao first, milk softening the edges, nothing clever required.
Now that belongs in a winter mug. Hot chocolate first, then that cool little mint finish after you swallow.
Mm! Peppermint-chocolate territory. If there were snow outside, I wouldn't be leaving this chair.
Orange hot chocolate. That's rich, fragrant, and just grown-up enough that I can pretend this isn't dessert.
Cinnamon in hot chocolate... this smells like the whole kitchen ought to be snowed in.
That's a very comforting mug, <player>. Cacao, warm milk, cinnamon. I don't need you to complicate it.
Oho! Cinnamon and a little cayenne in the cocoa. There's the warmth, and then there's the second warmth sneaking up behind it.
You've practically turned hot chocolate into pudding you can drink. The pinch of salt saves it from becoming too much.
Coconut hot chocolate. That's lush. It tastes like somebody smuggled a tropical holiday into a winter mug.
There we go! Marshmallow belongs on hot chocolate. Half of it melts into the cocoa and the rest sits there daring me to fish it out with a spoon.
Hot chocolate with marshmallow... yes, yes, completely predictable. I still want another mug.
No rum? I don't care. Lime, mint and sugar make a cracking little cooler all by themselves.
That's the sort of drink you finish and immediately start looking for the pitcher. Sharp lime, cold mint, done.
Strawberry lemonade. I would put a pitcher of that on the porch and lose track of how many glasses I'd had.
Oh, that's friendly. Proper lemonade underneath, fresh strawberry all through it. Nobody is arguing with this.
Raspberry lemonade has a little more bite to it. Tart, red, and wonderfully noisy on the tongue.
Whoa! Passionfruit and lime make you sit up straight. That's a tart little glass of trouble.
That's bright enough to wake the dead. I mean that as a compliment.
Look at that color! Pomegranate and lime tastes every bit as vivid as it looks.
Cranberry and orange with a little sweetness... breakfast juice has dressed itself up for company.
That is a gorgeous red drink. Hibiscus gives it a proper tart snap, and the orange keeps me coming back for another sip.
Mango and ginger has some movement to it. Sweet and thick at first, then that warm little kick catches up with you.
Yuzu, ginger and honey. If that doesn't wake you up, <player>, I don't know what will.
Pineapple, coconut and lime, with no rum anywhere in sight. Fine by me. This still tastes like a day off.
Tea and lemonade? Oh, that works. The tea makes it less childish without taking away the whole point of drinking lemonade.
Now that's a Mojito. Rum, lime, mint, sugar - clean, cold, and gone before you realize how strong it is.
Rum, lime, sugar. That's a Daiquiri, and it doesn't need a circus act around it. Nice and sharp.
Ah! A proper Daiquiri. Simple enough that there is nowhere for bad rum or tired lime to hide.
Now we're in punch territory. Rum, pineapple, orange, lime... pour this for a roomful of people and watch the bowl vanish.
Almond liqueur and lemon? Sweet, sour, and dangerously easy to finish. That's a very persuasive little drink.
Whiskey sour. There we are. The lemon wakes the whiskey right up, and the sugar keeps the whole thing civilized.
Brandy, orange liqueur, lemon. That's a Sidecar, all right - sharp suit, sharp drink.
Cream, cacao and brandy. That's dessert wearing evening clothes. Very smooth, very dangerous.
Whiskey and almond liqueur. Well, that's warmer and rounder than I expected. One of those drinks that gets quieter as the glass gets lower.
Brandy and almond liqueur is remarkably comfortable company. Nutty, warming, and absolutely an after-dinner sort of thing.
Butter in a drink sounds absurd right up until the rum, sugar and cinnamon arrive. Then suddenly I understand the entire idea.
Coffee liqueur in a milkshake? That's not a drink, that's a late-night dessert with a straw. Hand it over.
Orange liqueur in hot chocolate. Now you're making the cocoa wear a dinner jacket.
Whiskey in hot chocolate? That'll put some heat back in your fingers. Rich, boozy, and absolutely not for the children's table.
Pineapple, coconut and rum. You have made it physically impossible for me to think about work for the next five minutes.
Tea, honey and whiskey. That's medicine I would volunteer to take.
Allspice is already doing the work of three or four spices in one berry. This much turns warm and peppery into dusty and medicinal.
Hold on. I know it's called "allspice", but that doesn't mean you use ALL the spice, <player>!
Ah... ah... ACHOO! Great. Now my eyes are watering.
Mm. Apple and allspice. That's baked-apple territory straight away - warm and fragrant.
One pinch of allspice and the apple suddenly tastes as if somebody baked it. Fresh fruit in, warm oven smell out - lovely trick.
Ah, pumpkin with allspice. Now it tastes properly autumnal.
Mm. Pumpkin, warm allspice, little earthy finish. Very familiar, very good.
Orange and allspice. Smells like somebody has been simmering something for the holidays.
Mm. Allspice with orange peel - warm, bitter, fragrant. Nice.
Yum - that allspice brings back fond memories of some time I spent in the West Indies.
These two nuts make each other look good. Almond brings the clean crunch, pistachio brings the richer oil - I'd trust that combination in a gift box.
The almonds here are a timeless choice.
